title: Banjo players and Sweet Emma's start with Miss Caroline Benjamin
summary: Ridgley praises banjoists Tom Benton and John Marrero, then talks about pianist Sweet Emma and Miss Caroline Benjamin, who helped the band get started with society jobs.

story.theme_name: Medicine shows, minstrels, circuses and the black theater circuit
story.community_name: On the road with minstrel, carnival and tent shows

blocks.x: Well, we got along very good. You'd sing like that?
Yes, sing. It was really good.

Sometimes. Yeah, oh yeah. You'd do that, that action and all that was the funny things that you played. It was pretty good. Well, we got along very good. We had a wonderful, good banjo player. We had two in. Tom Benton was good. John Marrero was good. He was a banjo player and could sing and very good. He had piano piano, I know, routine as we called it. Couldn't read but he could play, he could cut it. Very good. And then the girl was good. She's still playing. She making money at her. Sweet Emma?
Yeah. I got a phone up I've been trying to get all yesterday.

She don't want to answer you. She wants that phone out of me. Tell me she's doing good. She's getting by one of the old tuxedo band people that had noticed and wanted a short bang, you know. And they didn't like her. Now who did give us our start with her was Miss Caroline Benjamin. St. John and Joseph Street. Now she was a good banjo, a guitar player and a good piano, a good musician. And her and several other young white girls. And they used to come around us when we played and they liked the way that Sweet Emma used to juggle that piano and different things like that. Well then when the people that helped give us our start and they told us they were going to help us and they just went along. They used to like to see us. She used to rock that piano. So I'd go see what no musician like those people were. But she was a very nice girl. And she helped us to get them in a good job. Because she always talked to the people nice to see when they come around.
